content: This is more of a "shower thought", and may be a silly question. I recently listened to a podcast that described proteins as "alien programs" (meaning we have the code for them, but by and large, we don't know what this code does). With regular code, we can prove things about it (like that an encoding and decoding algorithm round-trip). Can we similarly prove properties about proteins (or similar molecules like RNA) from their code in a way that is precise enough to write in Lean (when the relevant background is formalized)?

I know that the reason we can verify programs in human computer languages is that they have a known, deterministic, mathematically precise semantics. I don't know if there is anything like a semantics for proteins. And maybe proteins are more like robots, where one needs a model of the physical world they work in. (There is work on formalization in such cyber-physical settings, at least at the macro scale of human-made machines, but that is a lot more challenging.) Also, I know from AlphaFold that protein folding is hard, and I'm not sure there is any way to formally prove that a protein folds a certain way, or if one needs to know how a protein folds to know how it behaves.
One doesn't need to solve protein folding de novo, if you're working from a closely related protein, homology modeling is good enough!

Regarding protein as machines, look up NRPSs and PKSs, these are huge proteins that are basically assembly lines. It's a linear chain of domains each with a specific enzymatic function, like, add the next subunit, modify the most recently added subunit, prepare recent subunit for next addition step, etc. The addition domains encode which subunit they will add. Basically, if you read the DNA encoding this humongous gene, you can then read the protein AA sequence, which then can be interpreted as the chain of domains, which is an explicit recipe for the complex nonribosomal peptide or polyketide it will make.
This is a really cool evolutionary development where it is using higher and higher "levels of abstraction".

I do want to warn that this is not the norm. Even for something so canonical as the central dogma of DNA transcribed to mRNA then translated 3 bases at a time (codon) via tRNA and ribosome to protein... That isn't always true.

There is an essential yeast gene that has a coding region of length not divisible by 3. How? Well, the ribosome isn't infallible. It's a molecular machine and has its own failure modes, including accidental slippage, where it slips a base down the mRNA transcript. Usually this causes mistranslation or a stuck partial translation, and cellular garbage collection takes over.

But in the case of this one gene, near the end of the gene, there is a rare codon. That means the matching tRNA is not abundant in the cell. So while the ribosome waits at that codon, it's more likely to slip. And that slip is actually the expected outcome here. And then translation continues.
Is there a reason you'd want to formalize proteins themselves, as opposed to general biological pathways or gene "circuits"?

I would push back that proteins are programs. This seems like a related riff that somehow DNA is "source code". It's not. It's more like a memory region filled with bytecode and assembly, where depending on where you're reading and in what direction, you'll interpret entirely different instructions. And it is self editing. Reminds me of this Mario TAS where they do arbitrary code execution by literally running around the wrong part of memory and breaking blocks which represent values in the RAM thus modifying running code.

@Jason Rute  A variant of this idea that has been explored more extensively is to view networks of protein-protein interactions (i.e., collections of rules such as "protein A can bind protein B at site X when phosphorylated") as programs that can be verified and analyzed. There is a small community working on these topics, even with a dedicated conference (CMSB). I have done work in this area myself.

In both cases, a fundamental challenge is that biological systems are not the product of modular design but of a messy evolutionary process. Compositional reasoning is fundamental to programming language design and theorem proving, but many biological systems are hardly amenable to it. As a consequence, brute-force computational approaches such as model-checking have had more success so far than interactive theorem proving (but are fundamentally limited in terms of scalability).
Fascinating. Thanks for the insights!

I’m not personally interested in doing a project like this, but I was curious if it at all made sense. I am however vested in the broader question of what are all the real-world applications of theorem proving once we lower the barriers enough to make it x100 more scalable.

Sure. I see now how it is a leaky analogy. But I guess even in the Nintendo example, one could prove properties about how the dynamics behave from the initial bits. Like proving in certain games that certain bits can or can’t be modified. But at the same time I understand from you and @Jonathan Laurent that biology (at least in the protein level) doesn’t have the deterministic and modular structure that is strongly amenable to theorem proving, so again even the analogy with Nintendo games probably breaks down quickly.

I am however vested in the broader question of what are all the real-world applications of theorem proving once we lower the barriers enough to make it x100 more scalable.

Once the barriers are low enough, I can imagine interactive theorem proving having a significant impact on systems biology (and cell signalling in particular, as @Yakov Pechersky also suggests). None of the challenges I mentioned are unsolvable. Probabilistic programs can be reasoned about, non-modular systems can be rigorously approximated by modular ones, and theorem proving can be integrated with simulation and model checking.

At previous levels of automation, the juice was rarely worth the squeeze, and there was little hope of getting most biologists to use theorem provers. This may change rapidly, though.

@Yakov Pechersky These are nice anecdotes about the messiness (and beauty) of biology!

An undergrad, @Colin ⚛️ in my group, formalized the Central Dogma in Lean. We're putting final touches on the manuscript, here's the current draft:
BioLean.pdf

The way I think of it, is that we have a gap between experimental reality of biology and the conceptual models we imagine. The Central Dogma is such a model, and as such, we can work to formalize the conceptual model. As we formalize it, we're tasked with making those concepts precise, just as when one formalizes mathematics. But perhaps what's different from mathematics, is that we end up being forced to make some decisions about what we want our formalization to cover, in terms of what "sections" of the real world it ought to cover. In 4.1.1, we discuss accuracy - our rules don't cover differences in behavior between prokaryotes and eukaryotes, for example, or subtle differences that can be between species.

For me, I think the broader point is that all software for biology includes assumptions like this, they're just more often implicit, rather than explicit. It's weird to build software that can handle species-level exceptions to the triplet-->amino acid mapping, whatever language you'd write it in. If we want to computerize the task, it needs to be made rigid, and there are some nice things that Lean can do that Python or C cannot.

The yeast-ribosome-slippage example was relevant directly for me in my synthetic biology days, when we were developing codon optimization algorithms. Codon optimization is the idea that if I am going to express a protein from an inserted piece of DNA, due to the "non-injectivity" of translation, what is the best sequence to use? A naive approach is to use the most common codon for each AA, thus ensuring that tRNAs are abundant and translation isn't rate limited.

However, those sequences ended up being toxic sometimes. If you consider the DNA, it can be read 6 ways, forward at +0, +1, +2 offset, or reverse at 0, 1, 2. Native sequences, turn out, are much more likely to have stop codons appear in the non-canonical (+1, +2, -0, -1, -2) ways than the "canonical" reading frame. But our naive codon optimization algorithm did not have this -- and so transcripts that were in reverse, or ribosome slippage caused way more translation of undesired peptides -- especially since we were overexpressing the gene.

So I totally agree about the tradeoff on the assumptions vs reality situation. Perhaps where Lean and ITP style interactions can help most is in the maintenance / refactoring / expansion of such software systems to deal with more and more nuanced assumptions.
Oh, and also, powerful DSLs and macro systems to make it easier to express and embed certain concepts.
I played around with using diacritics/unicode combining characters to indicate base methylation/modification at one point.

For more protein related things, sound and verified alignment algorithms are critical in comparing proteins. I always cite this paper, about how worldwide, protein alignments were accidentally suboptimal due to mis-implementation of a published algorithm. https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/031500v1

Isn't the question whether we can formally verify something basically just "is it math"?
When it comes to proteins, Dill's hydrophobic-polar protein folding model is definitely math, and I formalized some of it here in connection with this paper.

Hi everyone,

I came across the thread about formalizing protein properties in Lean and found the discussion fascinating — especially the point about compositional reasoning being difficult in biology because biological systems aren't modularly designed.

I'd like to share something I've been working on that might be relevant to this conversation.

I have a background in molecular dynamics simulation and computational materials science. Recently, I developed a framework called "Gate & Channel" for interpreting the effects of missense mutations in the tumor suppressor protein TP53 (p53). The key idea is that instead of using machine learning to fit a continuous pathogenicity score, I wrote the entire classifier as a collection of explicit IF-THEN gates derived from physics and structural biology.

For example:

  • "IF residue is a direct Zn ligand AND substitution changes coordination chemistry, THEN gate = CLOSED"
  • "IF residue is in the MDM2-binding face (from crystal structure 1YCR) AND any substitution occurs, THEN gate = CLOSED"
  • "IF Gly→X in an intrinsically disordered region, THEN gate = CLOSED (loss of backbone freedom)"

Each gate tests one physical constraint. Gates are organized into independent channels (Parallel Causal Chains). A variant is predicted disruptive if any gate closes (n_closed >= 1). No weights are fitted, no thresholds are tuned against clinical labels.

The framework currently spans 11 channels with 30+ gates covering the full-length p53 protein, achieving 80.8% sensitivity and 89.1% PPV against ClinVar benchmarks — with zero fitted parameters.

What strikes me as potentially interesting for this community:

  1. The architecture is compositional by design. Adding a new gate never breaks existing gates, because channels are independent (PCC). This was empirically verified — when I added new IDR gates, zero previously correct predictions were lost.

  2. Each gate is a discrete, auditable IF-THEN proposition. It feels like these could be naturally expressed as Lean theorems — e.g., proving that a specific physical constraint necessarily leads to molecular disruption given certain structural premises.

  3. In principle, the full set of gates could converge to a complete physical description of why every possible mutation breaks (or doesn't break) a protein. This is fundamentally different from ML, where the ceiling is statistical approximation of training data.

The manuscript was just submitted to PLOS Computational Biology, and the code/data are publicly available:
https://github.com/miosync-masa/ZERO_parameter_1st_principles_GateFramework

I'm genuinely curious: does the idea of formalizing such physics-derived biological gates in Lean make sense to people here? Is this the kind of "real-world application" that could benefit from interactive theorem proving? I'd love to hear thoughts, pushback, or suggestions.
What do you mean by "closed"? Oncogenic?

Yakov Pechersky said:

What do you mean by "closed"? Oncogenic?

Good question! "CLOSED" means the gate has detected that a specific physical constraint is violated by the substitution — not oncogenic directly.

To be clear, I'm not claiming that proteins are programs or that this framework formalizes protein behavior itself. I think your earlier point in this thread is exactly right — proteins are far too messy and context-dependent for that.

What I'm formalizing is much narrower: "given this local structural/chemical context, does this specific amino acid substitution violate a known physical constraint?" For example:

  • Zn²⁺ in p53 is coordinated by C176, H179, C238, C242 at ~2.3Å. If you replace C176 with anything, the thiolate ligand is gone. That's not biology — that's coordination chemistry. Gate = CLOSED.

  • A proline-directed kinase recognizes [S/T]-P motifs. The cyclic imino ring of Pro IS the recognition element. Replace it, the kinase can't dock. That's enzyme-substrate geometry. Gate = CLOSED.

So each gate is really a statement about local physics/chemistry, not about the full complexity of the protein-as-machine. Whether that local disruption propagates to oncogenesis depends on penetrance, cellular context, redundancy, etc. — things the framework deliberately separates out.

The interesting part for this community might be: these local physical statements are compositional (independent channels, adding gates never breaks existing ones) and deterministic (no stochastic element, no fitted parameters). Which is exactly what makes them unlike protein behavior in general, but potentially amenable to formal reasoning.

And circling back to @Jason Rute's original question — I think the answer might be: formalizing the entire protein is probably out of reach (quantum mechanics + statistical mechanics + solvent effects + entropy + all interaction types in Lean 4 is... a lot). @Yakov Pechersky's point about the messiness of real biology and @Jonathan Laurent's point about compositionality both hold for that full problem.

But formalizing whether a specific substitution violates a specific local physical constraint — that IS math, and I think it's on the extension of what @Bjørn Kjos-Hanssen did with the HP model, just applied to real structural data rather than a lattice abstraction.

The thing that made me think this community might find it interesting is that tools like AlphaFold can predict structures remarkably well, but they're black boxes — you can't ask "why does this mutation break the protein?" and get an auditable answer. If the physical gates that answer "why" can be made explicit and formally verified, that seems like it would add something that pure ML approaches structurally cannot provide.

Before I get into it, I will give the disclaimer that the development of the project has involved a good amount of LLM-involvement, which I know can be concerning. Hopefully knowing that I am also experienced in fine-tuning my own models, running ablation studies, and coding gated harnesses will assuage some of those concerns.

Anyway, the entire project (red-hot_rebis) is built on my fork of the lean kernel that I expanded to paraconsistency (the edits I made are listed below)

The project features automated organic retrosyntheses, bespoke catalytic sites, RNA--->folded protein pipeline, even a materials engine. I'm pretty proud of it, it's a dream I've had 13 years in the making!

If you end up using it lmk, I'd love some feedback (which has been a bit of a surprising drought)

Here are the targeted edits I made to the kernel to make it paraconsistent :

Obviously, in your old fashioned glazed Lean, False.rec : (C : Sort u) → False → C allows deriving anything from a contradiction. This fork intercepts that at 3 points:

mods

  1. src/kernel/type_checker.cpp --- infer_constant rejects recursors for empty Prop inductives when paraconsistent = true
  2. src/library/constructions/cases_on.cpp --- casesOn generation blocked for empty Prop types
  3. src/kernel/environment.h --- is_paraconsistent() / mark_paraconsistent() methods added
  4. src/kernel/environment.cpp --- Extern C function implementations for Lean FFI
  5. src/Lean/Environment.lean --- paraconsistent : Bool field + Kernel.Environment.markParaconsistent
  6. src/Init/Paraconsistent.lean --- New: User-facing module with enableParaconsistent and Belnap FOUR

blocked

  1. False.elim : (C : Sort u) → False → C
  2. False.rec : (C : Sort u) → False → C
  3. False.casesOn : (C : Sort u) → False → C
  4. absurd : (h₁ : a) → (h₂ : ¬a) → b
  5. Any match h with . where h : False

remains

  1. False is still defined; it simply cannot eliminate into other types
  2. All other logical connectives (True, And, Or, Eq, etc.) are unaffected
  3. The entire standard library works when paraconsistent mode is off
  4. Contradictions are tolerated without trivializing the system
